div.p: The messenger whom you sent to announce the death of our little child seems to have missed me on his way to Athens; but when I came to Tanagra I learned of it from my granddaughter. As for the matters concerning the funeral, I think they have already taken place; and may what has been done be such as will be least painful to you both now and for the future. But if there is something you wished to do and have not done, but are waiting for my opinion, and you think you will bear it more lightly once it is done, this too shall be, without any excess and superstition, of which you have the least share of anyone.

Only, wife, keep me too καμὲ] κἄμ’ ἐν? in our affliction, and yourself, in a settled state. καθεστῶτος] γεγονότος codex C For I myself know and measure how great our loss is; but if I find you exceeding all bounds in your distress, this will trouble me more than what has happened. And yet καίτοι γʼ? I myself was not born from oak or from rock cf. Hom. τ 163, and you know it yourself, having shared with me in the rearing of so many children παιδίων *: παίδων. cf. paulo post τὰ τηλικαῦτα , all of whom were brought up at home by ourselves.
This one τούτου *: τούτοις was especially dear to me, because a daughter was born to you, who longed for one, after four sons, and because she gave me the longed-for ποθούμενον *: ποιούμενον occasion to bestow your name on her ἐν αὐτῇ] malim ἑαυτῇ . There is also a peculiar poignancy in our affection for children of that age, and the delight they give αὐτῶν scripsi ex αὐτὸν, idem voluerat Stegmannus is pure and unmixed with any anger or reproach. She herself αὕτη idem: αὐτὴ also had by nature a wonderful good temper and gentleness, and her way of returning love and of giving pleasure gave us delight and at the same time an insight into her kindness; for she used to bid her nurse τίτθην *: τιτθὴν give and offer the breast not only to other infants but even to the objects she took pleasure in and to her toys, and out of kindness she invited them as it were to her own table, sharing the most pleasant of whatever ὦνπερ *: ὥσπερ she knew and had with the things that gave her pleasure.

But I do not see, wife, why these things and the like, which delighted us while she lived, should now grieve and trouble us when we call them to mind. But again I am also afraid that together with what pains us we may cast out the memory, like Clymene, who says
And I hate the well-held μισῶ δ’ ἀγκύλον idem Nauck. p. 612
bow of cornel-wood, and δʼ] τʼ Keilius let the sports be gone οἰχοίατο Emperius always fleeing from and trembling at the reminder of her son, because it brought grief λύπην idem: αὐτὴν with it; for nature flees everything that is distasteful.
For just as she herself offered herself to us as the sweetest of all things to embrace, to see and to hear, so too the thought of her must dwell and live with us, bringing more joy than grief, or rather many times more; if indeed it is reasonable that some of the arguments which we have often spoken to others should be of use to us too at the right time, and that we should not sit idle or shut ourselves in, giving in return for those pleasures griefs many times as great.

And this too those who were present report in amazement, that you did not even change into mourning clothes, nor brought any neglect ἀτημέλειαν *: ἑτιμέλειαν upon yourself or your maidservants; nor was there any preparation of festive extravagance at the funeral, but everything was done decorously and in silence with our closest kin. I for my part did not wonder at this, that you, who never adorned yourself for theatre or procession but held extravagance useless even for pleasures, kept in sad circumstances your simplicity ἀφελὲς R: ἀσφαλὲς and frugality. For not only in Bacchic revels βακχεύμασι] Eur. Bacch. 317 must the chaste woman remain uncorrupted, but she must think that the turmoil in grief and the agitation of emotion need, no less ἦττον οἴεσθαι Benselerus, a self-control that contends not against parental love, as most people think, but against the intemperance of the soul. For to parental love we grant the longing for, the honouring and the remembering of those who are gone; but the insatiable desire for lamentation, which leads on to wailing and beating of the breast, is no less shameful than incontinence in pleasures.
Yet in argument λόγῳ] ἀλόγως R it has met with pardon, because what is painful and bitter in it, instead of what is pleasant, is attached to the shameful. For what is more unreasonable than to cut away excesses of laughter and exuberant joy, but to give free rein entirely to the streams of weeping and wailing that flow from one and the same source? Or that some men quarrel with their wives over perfume and purple, but allow them mourning haircuts, and the dyeing of their clothes black μελαίνας R: μελαίνης , and unsightly sitting and painful lying down? And, what is hardest of all, if the women punish servants or maidservants beyond measure and unjustly, they oppose and stop them, but overlook them when they are cruelly and bitterly punished by themselves, in sufferings and misfortunes that call for relief and kindness?

But between us, wife, there has been no need of that battle with each other, nor, I think, will there be need of this one. For with your frugality in dress and the plainness of your way of life there is none of the philosophers who has come into our company and acquaintance whom you have not astonished; nor οὐδὲ Stegmannus: οὔτε any of the citizens to whom you do not present παρέσχες? your own simplicity as a spectacle at rites and sacrifices and theatres. And before now too you showed great steadiness in such matters, when you lost the eldest of our children; and again, when our handsome Chaeron Χαιρωνος X: χάρωνος left us. For I remember that strangers were travelling with me from the sea when the death of the child was announced, and that they came along with the others to the house.
But when they saw the great orderliness and quiet, as they later related to others too, they thought that nothing terrible had happened, but that an empty report had been spread for no reason; so wisely had you ordered the house at a time that gave much licence for disorder, although you had nursed that child at your own breast ἐξέθρεψας μασθῷ Benselerus and had endured the lancing of your nipple when it was bruised; for these are noble things and marks of a loving mother.

But most mothers, we see, when their little children have been washed and made bright by others, take them into their arms like playthings, and then, when they die, pour themselves out into empty and thankless mourning, not out of affection (for affection is reasonable and good), but ἀλλὰ] ἀλλ’ ὅτι? the craving for empty repute, mixed in great measure with the little natural feeling, makes the τὰ R mourning savage, frantic and hard to appease. And this, it seems, did not escape Aesop; for he said that when Zeus was distributing honours to the gods, Grief too asked for one. cf. p. 112 a So he gave it to him, but only among those who choose it and are willing. In the beginning, then, this is how it happens: each person brings grief in upon himself. But once it has become established ἰδρυθῇ Duebnerus: ἱδρυνθῇ with time and has become a companion and housemate, it does not leave even when people very much wish it to. Therefore one must fight it at περὶ] malim παρὰ the doors and not admit it with a guard of mourning clothes or cropped hair or any other such thing.
For these, confronting us every day and putting us to shame, make the mind petty, narrow, shut in, implacable ἀμείλικτον] ἄμικτον Doehnerus and fearful of every sound, so that it has no part any longer in laughter or light or a friendly table, since it wears and handles such things because of its grief. Neglect of the body follows upon this evil, and aversion to anointing and bathing and the rest of one's daily regimen; whereas quite the contrary was needed, that the soul, when it is suffering, should itself be helped by the body being strong. For much of what pains us is blunted and slackened, like a wave in fair weather, when it is dispersed in the calm of the body. But if dryness and roughness arise from a bad regimen, and the body sends up to the soul nothing kindly or wholesome but only pains and griefs, like bitter and noxious exhalations, then it is no longer easy to recover, even for those who wish to. Such are the afflictions that seize the soul when it has been so badly treated.

And indeed, what is greatest and most to be feared in this matter I would not fear: the visits of bad women κακῶν γυναικῶν εἰσοδους] cf. Eur. Andr. 930 and their cries and joint lamentations, which chafe and whet the grief, not allowing it to wither away either through others or of itself. For I know what struggles you recently fought, helping the sister of Theon and battling the women who came in from outside with wailings and shrieks, simply bringing, as it were, fire upon fire.
For when people see the houses of their friends on fire, they put them out, each with all the speed and strength he has; but to souls that are aflame they themselves ταῖς δὲ ψυχαῖς φλεγομέναις αὐτοὶ R: τὰς δὲ ψυχὰς φλεγομένας αὐτοῖς bring kindling. And they do not allow anyone who wishes to put his hands to a man with sore eyes, nor do they touch the inflamed part; but the mourner sits offering to everyone who comes along his affliction, like a flux ῥεῦμα] τραῦμα Kaltwasserus, to stir up and make savage, so that from a small tickling and irritation it is chafed into a great and grievous malady. ἀναξαινόμενον R: ἀναξηραινομενον But I know that you will guard against these things.

Try, carrying yourself back in thought, to set yourself often in that time when, this child not yet having been born, we had no complaint against fortune; then join this present time to that one, as though the circumstances around us had become the same again. For otherwise, wife, we shall seem to resent the birth of the child, if we make the state of things before she was born more free from complaint for ourselves. The two years in between we must not remove from our memory, but, since they gave us joy and enjoyment, we must count them among our pleasures; and we must not consider the small good a great evil, nor, because fortune did not add what we hoped for, be ungrateful also for what was given. For reverent speech towards the divine and a cheerful and uncomplaining attitude towards fortune always yield a fair and sweet fruit.
And in such circumstances he who most of all draws from the memory τῇ μνήμῃ R of his blessings, and turns his mind towards the bright and shining parts of his life and carries it away from the dark and troubling ones, either quenches his grief entirely or, by mixing it with its opposite, makes it small and faint. For just as perfume always delights the sense of smell but is also a remedy against foul odours, so the thought of good things in bad times also καὶ] del. R provides the service of a needed remedy to those who do not shun the remembrance of their blessings nor blame fortune for everything and in every way. It does not befit us to suffer what happens to those who slander their own life if, like a book, it has one blot while all the rest is clean and unspoiled.

For you have often heard that happiness depends on right reasoning ending in a stable disposition, and that the turns of fortune do not cause great deviations nor bring confounding συγχυτικὰς R: συντυχικὰς slips in our life. But if we too, like the many, must be steered by external things and count up the gifts of fortune and use any chance people as judges of our happiness, do not look at the present tears and lamentations of those coming in, performed out of some bad custom towards everyone, but consider rather how you continue to be envied by these very people for your children and your home and your life. And it is a terrible thing that others would gladly choose your lot even with this added over which we are now grieving.
And it is terrible that you should complain and be distressed at it as it is, and not even perceive, from the very thing that stings, how great a delight the things that are preserved still hold for us; but that, like those who pick out the headless and tapering lines of Homer but entirely overlook the many great parts of his poems, you should scrutinize and malign the bad things of your life, and attend to the good ones vaguely and confusedly, and so suffer something like the mean and avaricious, who gather much but do not use it while they have it, and lament and are distressed when it is lost. But if you feel pity for her because she has gone unmarried and childless, you can in turn give yourself pleasure in other things, since you have not been without any of these nor had no share in them ἀτελοῦς μηδ’ ἀμοίρου γενομένης W; for these things cannot be great goods for those deprived of them and small for those who have them. And she, having arrived where there is no pain, has no need for us to grieve; for what harm comes to us from her, if nothing now is painful to her? For even the loss of great things loses its pain when it has come to the point of no longer needing them. περιγενόμεναι R: παραγενόμεναι Your Timoxena has been deprived of small things, for she knew small things and delighted in small things; but things of which she had neither perception nor any notion, οὔτ’ εἰς ἐπίνοιαν ἦλθεν οὔτ’ ἔλαβεν ἐπίνοιαν. cf. p. 608 d how could she be said to be deprived of them?

And indeed, as for what you hear from others, who persuade many by saying that nothing in any way is evil or painful to one who has been dissolved, I know that you are kept from believing it.
For the teaching of our fathers prevents it, and the mystic symbols of the rites of Dionysus, which we who share in them know together with one another. Consider, then, that the soul, being imperishable, is affected in the same way as birds that are caught: if it has been reared in the body for a long time and has become tame to this life through many affairs and long familiarity, it alights again and enters once more into a body, and does not give up or cease becoming entangled in the passions and fortunes of this world through its births. For do not think that old age is reviled and ill spoken of because of its wrinkles and grey hair and the weakness of the body; but this is the hardest thing about it, that it makes the soul stale in its memories of the things there and clinging to the things here, and bends and presses it down, as it keeps the shape that it took on from the body in being affected πεπονθέναι] προσπεπονθέναι R, preserving it. διαφυλάττουσαν idem: διαφυλάττουσα But the soul that is taken locum lacunosam (90 fere litt. E) redintegravit W ita: ἡ δὲ ληφθεῖσα μέν, μένουσα δὲ βρα χὺν ἐν τῷ σώματι χρόνον ἐλευθερωθεῖσα ὑπὸ κρειττόνων ἔρχεται - πρὸς ὃ πέφυκεν is held by higher powers, as though springing back ἀναχαιτίσασα W: ἀναχαίτισμα from a supple and soft bend to its natural state. For just as fire, if one puts it out and at once lights it again, is fanned up again and quickly recovers lac. 148 fere in E fort. supplenda hunc in modum: καὶ ἀναλαμβάνει ταχέως· κατασβεσθὲν δὲ καὶ ὑποψυχθὲν οὐκ ἄν τις ἀναζωπυρήσειεν (vel πάλιν ἐξάψειεν cf. p. 787 a) ἀπραγμόνως· οὕτω καὶ τῶν ψυχῶν ἄριστα πράττουσιν, αἶς συμβέβηκε κατὰ τὸν ποιητήν ὅπως ὤκιστα cett. as quickly as possible ὅπως ὤκιστα] cf. Bergk. 2 p. 156 to pass the gates of Hades before πρὶν R: πλὴν a great love of the things here arises in them, and they are softened towards the body and fused with it as if by drugs.

But in our ancestral and ancient customs and laws the truth about these things is shown more clearly. For people do not bring libations to their own infants who have died, nor do they perform for them the other rites that it is fitting εἰκὸς] ἔθος Cobetus for the rest ἄλλους] ἀνθρώπους F. Schmidtius to perform on behalf of the dead; for they have no share in earth, nor οὐδὲ Stegmannus: οὔτε in earthly things. Nor do people linger there about their burials and tombs and the laying-out of their dead, and sit by their bodies; for the laws do not allow them to mourn θρηνεῖν addidi cum R for those of such an age, since it is not holy to do so for those who have passed into a better and more divine lot and place lac. 52 fere in E supplet W ita: καὶ οὐκ ἀγνοῶ μὲν ὅτι ταῦτα πολλὰς ἔχει ἀπορίας· ἐπεὶ δὲ cett.. Since, then, disbelieving them is harder than believing, let us keep our outward conduct as the laws command, and our inner life still more unstained, pure and self-controlled. σώφρονα] intell. ἔχωμεν
